body_md: To more than one person, a command ends in **-en** for -ar verbs and in **-an** for the rest: **pasen**, **esperen**, **vengan**, **traigan**. A pronoun sticks to the end: **siéntense**.
A porteño host says **pasen, pasen** at the door, **pónganse cómodos**, and **no se preocupen** when you apologise for being late.
**Me da miedo** is *it scares me* in general; **me dio miedo** is one scare, over and done. The thing that scares you is the subject: **me dan miedo los perros**.
**Boludo** is common between close friends and an insult to anyone else — understand it, don't use it yet. **Quilombo** means a mess; it's informal, not rude, but keep it out of formal settings.
*de + el* always becomes **del**, and *a + el* becomes **al**: *la parada del bondi*, *voy al centro*.
For more than one person: **pasen**, **vengan**, **siéntense**, **no se preocupen**.
To say who you are, use **soy**: *Soy Sofi.* One word carries "I am" — Spanish has no separate word for "I" here.

Three people, three forms of *ser*:

| yo | **soy** |
| vos | **sos** |
| él, ella | **es** |

The verb already tells you who, so the pronoun is usually dropped: *Es de Rosario* — he's (or she's) from Rosario.
For more than one person, Argentina uses **ustedes** with the same verb form as *ellos*: *ustedes son*, *ellos son*.

| **Tendría que haber** ido. | I should have gone. |
| **Tendrías que haber** avisado. | You should have let us know. |
| **Me arrepiento.** | I regret it. |

**Tendría que haber** + participle: the porteño regret. Never *he debido*.
**Acabo de** + infinitive is *I just did it*: **acabo de llegar**, **acaba de salir**. **Volví a** is *I did it again*: **volví a perder las llaves**. Or just **de nuevo**.
One person **ceba** — pours the water from the **termo** — and passes the mate around the **ronda**. You drink it all, through the **bombilla**, and hand it back to the one who ceba.
**Me siento mal** — *I feel bad*. **Lo siento** — *I'm sorry*, for real bad news. For bumping into someone, say **perdón**.
You meet this form after *si* and after *ojalá* — **ojalá pudiera** — and almost nowhere else at this level.

| yo, él, ella | **hubiera** | sabido, venido, ido |
| vos | **hubieras** | llamado, avisado, pensado |

For what didn't happen, both halves: **Si hubiera sabido, te hubiera avisado.** *If I'd known, I'd have told you.* Compare *si supiera* — if I knew (now).

| | ir, ser | estar | tener |
| yo | **fui** | **estuve** | **tuve** |
| vos | **fuiste** | **estuviste** | **tuviste** |
| él, ella | **fue** | **estuvo** | **tuvo** |
| nosotros | **fuimos** | | |
| ellos | **fueron** | | |

No accents here. *Fui a la cancha* is *went*; *fue bárbaro* is *was*.
The feeling verbs keep their pronoun in the past too: **me enojé**, **te asustaste**, **se preocupó**.
**Quiero ir** — *I want to go*. **Quiero que vayas** — *I want you to go*. When the wish is about someone else, the second verb turns subjunctive.

| what he said | what you tell |
| «Voy.» | Dijo que **iría**. |
| «Vengo mañana.» | Dijo que **vendría** mañana. |
| «Te llamo.» | Dijo que me **llamaría**. |

A promise told later goes into *would*. Just as porteño: **dijo que iba a venir**.
**Facturas** are the pastries you buy by the dozen at the bakery — *medialunas* are the best known. Nothing to do with bills.
With a vos command the pronoun joins the end: **ayudame**, **alcanzame** — *help me*, *hand me*.

| | -ar | -er, -ir |
| yo | labur**é** | com**í**, sal**í** |
| vos | labur**aste** | com**iste**, sal**iste** |
| él, ella | labur**ó** | com**ió**, sal**ió** |
| nosotros | | com**imos**, sal**imos** |

-er and -ir share one set of endings. *Salimos* is both *we go out* and *we went out* — *anoche* or *ayer* tells you which.

title_en: Se me, se te, se le
body_md:
| to me | **se me** cayó | I dropped it |
| to you | **se te** cayó | you dropped it |
| to him, her | **se le** cayó | he dropped it |

Same with *rompió, perdió, olvidó*: **se me olvidó** — *I forgot*. The middle word says who it happened to.
A strike is a **paro**: **hay paro de subte**, **paro de colectivos**. When protesters block a street it's a **piquete** or a **corte**, and the street **está cortada**. A **marcha** is a march.
A reaction to someone else's news takes the subjunctive: **qué bueno que estés acá**, **me alegro que te vaya bien**, **qué lástima que no puedas venir**.

| | regular | shortened |
| yo, él, ella | comprar**ía**, ir**ía** | **tendría**, **podría**, **haría**, **diría** |
| vos | ir**ías** | |

The ending goes on the whole infinitive: *comprar* → **compraría**. **Yo que vos** + would is advice: *yo que vos, esperaría*.

*Tener* — to have — is how you give your age:

| yo | **tengo** | Tengo veinte años. |
| vos | **tenés** | ¿Cuántos años tenés? |
| él, ella | **tiene** | Tiene doce años. |

The *e* of *tener* becomes *ie* in *tiene* — but never in the vos form: **tenés**.
Argentines buy almost anything **en cuotas** — in instalments — and the first question at the till is **¿en cuántas cuotas?**
**Hacer** + infinitive is *to make someone do*: **me hizo reír**, **me hizo llorar**, **nos hizo esperar**. **Me hace acordar** — *it reminds me*: *esta canción me hace acordar a vos*.
Adjectives match their noun: *remera linda*, *zapatillas lindas*. **Re** in front of an adjective means *really*: *re lindo*. And **chico** means *small*.
**Entre nos** — *between you and me* — is where porteño gossip starts. **Sin querer** — *by accident*: **te pisé sin querer**.
**¿De qué cuadro sos?** — and the answer is for life.
**Era otra época** — *it was a different time*. The **inmigrantes** of the early 20th century built the city's **conventillos**, its tango and its accent.

| a habit — normal verb | not yet — subjunctive |
| Cuando **llego**, tomo mate. | Avisame cuando **llegues**. |
| Cuando **termino**, salgo. | Cuando **termines**, llamame. |

About the future, *cuando* and **apenas** take the subjunctive: *apenas puedas*.
*Me levanto, te levantás, se levanta* — the pronoun comes before the verb and matches the person. **Los sábados** means *on Saturdays*.
For machines, porteños say **anda** — *it works*: **no anda el wifi**, **¿anda el ascensor?**. *Funciona* is fine, just stiffer.

The verb matches the thing you like, not you:

| one thing | more than one |
| Me **gusta** el mate. | Me **gustan** las facturas. |
| ¿Te **gusta** la milanesa? | ¿Te **gustan** los mates? |

**Me** — to me, **te** — to you, **le** — to him or her. For emphasis, add *a mí*: *A mí me gusta amargo.*
**Trucho** — *fake, dodgy*: *un billete trucho*. **Zarpado** — *over the top*, for good or bad. **Bardo** — *a mess, trouble*: *se armó un bardo*.
The shortest way to order anything: name it and add **por favor**. *Un café, por favor.* *Una medialuna, por favor.* No verb needed.
The porteño sign-off, in emails and out of them: **cualquier cosa, avisame** — *if anything comes up, let me know*. A **consulta** is a question you send; a **respuesta**, the reply.
**Enterarse** is *to find out, to hear about*: **me enteré ayer**, **¿te enteraste?**, **se enteró todo el mundo**.
**Sé** (with an accent) is *I know*. **¿Sabés?** — *do you know?* And the porteño *I have no idea*: **ni idea**.

| **Acabo de** llegar. | I just got here. |
| **Suelo** almorzar tarde. | I usually have lunch late. |
| **Volví a** perder las llaves. | I lost my keys again. |

All three take an infinitive. **Soler** has no past you'll need: *antes almorzaba tarde* does the job.
**Me siento mal** — *I feel ill*; **¿cómo te sentís?** — *how do you feel?* On its own, **lo siento** is *I'm sorry*.

| straight out | softer |
| Probá el flan. | Te recomiendo que **pruebes** el flan. |
| Pedí un taxi. | Es mejor que **pidas** un taxi. |

**Te recomiendo que** and **es mejor que** take the subjunctive. *Probar* → **pruebes**, *pedir* → **pidas**.
Carlos **Gardel** died in 1935, and porteños still say he **canta mejor cada día**. A tango's **letra** — *lyrics* — is usually about **nostalgia**: the barrio, the mother, the woman who left.
**Quería que vinieras** puts the wish in the past, so the second verb follows it. **Aunque** takes the subjunctive only for a maybe: *aunque llueva*.
**Recorrer** is *to travel around, to go all over*: **recorrimos la Patagonia**. The road is the **ruta** — *la ruta 40* runs the length of the country.

| yo, él, ella | **había** | comido, llegado, salido |
| vos | **habías** | hecho, dicho, visto |
| ellos | **habían** | |

One past behind another: **Cuando llegué, ya habían comido.** *Hecho, dicho, visto* are the irregular ones.
**No hace falta** — *there's no need*. **Conviene** is the advice: **conviene ir temprano** — *it's best to go early*.
On its own, **es que…** is the start of every porteño excuse: **¿no venís? — Es que laburo temprano**.
The politest way to ask is **quisiera** — *I'd like*: **quisiera un turno**. **Disculpe** gets attention, **le agradezco** says thank you. To a friend: **disculpá**, **te agradezco**.

| **Cuanto más** practicás, | The more you practice, |
| mejor hablás. | the better you speak. |
| Avisame **cuanto antes**. | Let me know as soon as you can. |

**Cuanto más** + one thing, then the other with **más**, **menos**, **mejor**.
**Bondi** is the everyday word for the city bus; *colectivo* is the neutral one. The **subte** is the Buenos Aires underground.
Flats are sized in **ambientes** — rooms, not counting the kitchen and bathroom. *Un dos ambientes* has a living room and one bedroom.
**Yo que vos** — *if I were you* — is how a porteño gives advice, and the conditional follows: **yo que vos, iría**, **yo que vos, no diría nada**.
**La verdad** opens an honest answer: **la verdad, no sé** — *honestly, I don't know*. **La verdad que sí** — *yeah, really*.
The imperfect paints the scene, the preterite is what happens in it: **Estaba en el subte cuando me llamó Sofi** — *I was on the subway when Sofi called me*.
**No me alcanza** — *it's not enough (for me)*. It works for money, time, anything: **no me alcanza la plata**, **no me alcanza el tiempo**.
Use **estar** for how you are right now: *estoy cansado*, *¿estás nerviosa?* The adjective matches the person: *cansado* for a man, *cansada* for a woman.
**Creo que viene** — the indicative, because you believe it. **No creo que venga** — the subjunctive, because you doubt it.
**Facu** is short for *facultad* — university. For jobs, Spanish drops the article: **Soy profesora**, not *soy una profesora*.
**Para** + an infinitive when it's the same person: *estudio para aprender*. **Para que** + the subjunctive when it's someone else: **te lo mando para que lo leas**.

A little **la** that points at nothing turns a verb into an idiom: **se la cree** — *he's full of himself*; **me la banco** — *I can handle it*; **la tenés clara** — *you know your stuff*. With **las**: **me las arreglo** — *I get by*.

| | now | yesterday |
| yo | labur**o** | labur**é** |
| vos | labur**ás** | labur**aste** |
| él, ella | labur**a** | labur**ó** |

*Laburo* is *I work*; **laburó** is *he worked*. Only the stress, and the accent that marks it, tells them apart. Every regular -ar verb works like this: *hablé, llegaste, compró*.

title_en: Aunque: a fact, or a maybe
body_md: **Aunque llueve, vamos** — it's raining, and we're going. **Aunque llueva, vamos** — whether it rains or not. A fact takes the normal verb; a maybe takes the subjunctive.

| not found yet — subjunctive | already found — normal verb |
| Busco un depto que **tenga** balcón. | Encontré un depto que **tiene** balcón. |
| Busco algo que **quede** cerca. | Vivo en un depto que **queda** cerca. |
| ¿Hay un dueño que **acepte** mascotas? | Mi dueño **acepta** mascotas. |

If it might not even exist, the verb after **que** goes into the subjunctive.
Something you're looking for but haven't found yet takes the subjunctive: **busco un depto que tenga balcón**. Once you've found it, it doesn't: *encontré un depto que tiene balcón*.
English says *used to*; Spanish just uses the imperfect. **Jugábamos en la calle** — *we used to play in the street*. **Siempre**, **a veces** and **de chico** go with it.
An argument in Buenos Aires is a sport, not a fight: **discutimos** a lot and stay friends. **Me convenciste** — *you've convinced me*; **cambié de idea** — *I changed my mind*.
The verb already says who: *soy* is only ever "I am", *sos* only "you are". So **Soy de acá** and *Yo soy de acá* are both right, and the short one is what people say.
Spanish says you *have* years: **Tengo veinte años** — I'm twenty. *Tenés* is the vos form, *tiene* is for him or her.

| | ponerse | enojarse |
| yo | **me puse** | **me enojé** |
| vos | **te pusiste** | **te enojaste** |
| él, ella | **se puso** | **se enojó** |

The pronoun stays in the past. **Ponerse** + a feeling is *to get*: *me puse nervioso* — *I got nervous*.

| Mi prima **se casó** el sábado. | got married |
| **Nos casamos** en marzo. | we got married |
| El bebé **nació** ayer. | was born |
| ¿Dónde **naciste**? | were you born |

**Casarse** takes its pronoun; **nacer** doesn't.
**Ya no** is *not anymore*: **ya no vivo ahí**. **Cada vez más** — *more and more*: **cada vez más caro**; **cada vez menos** — *less and less*.
The tip is **la propina**, usually ten per cent and in cash. **¿Compartimos?** — *shall we share?* — is how two people order one enormous *bife*.

| yo | **estoy** |
| vos | **estás** |
| él, ella | **está** |

Two verbs mean *to be*. **Ser** says who or what something is, and where it's from: *Soy de Rosario.* **Estar** says where it is right now: *Estoy en el centro.*
**Llevarse bien** is *to get along*: **me llevo bien con mi hermana**, **nos llevamos re mal**.

title_en: One word for yo and él
body_md: **Venga**, **vaya**, **haga** are both *I* and *he/she*: *quiere que venga* — *he wants me/him to come*. The *que* and the context tell you who.
**Fue** + participle, agreeing: **fue construido**, **fue inaugurada**, **fueron detenidos**.
**Se me cayó el vaso** — the glass fell, and it happened to me. No blame: that is why every porteño story of a mishap starts with **se me**.
The card for the bus and the subte is **la SUBE**, and you **cargás** it at a kiosco — the same verb as charging a phone.
**Donde** with no accent joins a place to the rest of the sentence: **el bar donde nos conocimos** — *the bar where we met*. The question keeps its accent: *¿dónde?*
Report what someone said and the tense steps back: **viene** becomes **dijo que venía**.

| | hacer | ver | decir | venir | poder |
| yo | hice | vi | dije | vine | pude |
| vos | hiciste | viste | dijiste | viniste | pudiste |
| él, ella | hizo | vio | dijo | | |

A new stem, then *-e, -iste, -o* — with no accent. Tell the story in order with **primero**, **entonces**, **al final**.
Nobody says *quisiera*: **dame un kilo de papas** — *give me a kilo of potatoes* — is polite enough with a *por favor*.
**Insistió en que fuera** — *she insisted I go*. **Me sugirió que la llamara** — *he suggested I call her*. Same pattern: the verb after **que** in the past subjunctive.

| Acá **se cena** tarde. | People eat late here. |
| **Se saluda** con un beso. | You greet with a kiss. |

**Se** + the *él* form talks about everyone in general, no one in particular.
**Estar por** + infinitive is *to be about to*: **estoy por salir** — *I'm just about to leave*. A porteño's *I'm on my way* is often **ya salgo**, which may mean in an hour.
**Prohibido estacionar** — *no parking*; **prohibido fumar** — *no smoking*. The sign itself is a **cartel**.
**Boludo** is common between close friends and an insult to anyone else — understand it, don't use it yet. **Quilombo** means a mess; it's informal, not rude, but keep it out of formal settings.

title_en: Quiero que + a new verb form
body_md: When you want *someone else* to do something, the second verb changes: **quiero que vengas** — *I want you to come*. This form is the **subjunctive**, and *querer que* is where it starts.
**Me toca a mí** — *it's my turn*. **¿A quién le toca?** — *whose turn is it?* The chore follows as it is: **te toca lavar los platos**.
The softest porteño suggestion is **estaría bueno** — *it would be nice*: **estaría bueno juntarnos**, **estaría bueno que vengas**. **Habría que** is *we ought to*: *habría que avisarle*.
**Acabo de** — just now; **suelo** — usually; **volví a** — again.
**¿Qué te parece?** — *what do you think?* — and the answer **me parece bien**, **me parece que no**.

title_en: Today or yesterday: the stress tells
body_md: **Hoy laburo**, **ayer laburé**. The same verb, and only the stress moves: *LA-bu-ro* is now, *la-bu-RÉ* is done. Say it out loud and the past is already right.
**Me prometiste que vendrías** — *you promised me you'd come*. And the classic ending: **al final no vino**.
For what didn't happen: **si hubiera sabido, te hubiera avisado** — *if I'd known, I'd have told you*. Porteños use **hubiera** + a participle in both halves.
**¿Tenés la tarjeta? Sí, la tengo.** The pronoun stands for the thing and goes before the verb: *lo* and *los* for masculine words, *la* and *las* for feminine ones.
**Me robaron el celu** — *my phone got stolen*, literally *they stole the phone from me*. The thief is a **chorro** in lunfardo, a **ladrón** in the news.
On the 29th of every month many families eat **ñoquis** with a banknote under the plate, for luck. A **feriado** is a public holiday, and there are plenty of them.
**Crecer** is *to grow* — a city, a kid, a tree: **el barrio creció**, **crecí en Rosario** — *I grew up in Rosario*. The new towers are **edificios**.
Buenos Aires is a grid of **avenidas** — Corrientes, Santa Fe, 9 de Julio — and every corner has a **semáforo**. Cross when it's green: **cruzá**.

Take off *-ar* and add the ending for the person:

| yo | labur**o** |
| vos | labur**ás** |
| él, ella | labur**a** |
| nosotros | labur**amos** |
| ellos, ustedes | labur**an** |

It works for *hablar, tomar, estudiar, caminar* — every regular -ar verb. **Hacer** is irregular in *yo*: **hago**, *hacés, hace*.
For plans, porteños use **voy a** + verb far more than the future: **la semana que viene voy a descansar**. **Pienso** and **tengo ganas de** do the same job.
**Vale la pena** — *it's worth it*. The highest praise a porteño gives a place.

| Creo que **es** así. | No creo que **sea** así. |
| Creo que **está** en casa. | No creo que **esté** en casa. |
| Creo que **tiene** razón. | No creo que **tenga** razón. |
| Creo que **hay** tiempo. | No creo que **haya** tiempo. |

Sure → the normal verb. Doubting → the subjunctive.
**Entregar el proyecto** before the **plazo**; **plantear** the raise you **merecés**.
Lunfardo is Buenos Aires slang, born in the port and the tango: **morfar** (to eat), **guita** (money), **fiaca** (laziness), **pilcha** (clothes). Friends, not job interviews.
**Tengo ganas de ir a la playa** — *I feel like going to the beach*. **Pienso ir** — *I'm planning to go*.
**Se** + a verb says what people do in general: **acá se cena tarde** — *people have dinner late here*; **se saluda con un beso** — *you greet with a kiss*.
**Recién llegué** — *I just got here*. A porteño uses *recién* with the plain past where English says *just*.
**¿Dónde estará?** is not about tomorrow: it is *I wonder where he is*. The future guesses; **capaz** and **seguro que** do it in the present.
**Cuando llegás, me avisás** is a habit; **cuando llegues, avisame** is one future time. For what hasn't happened yet, *cuando* takes the subjunctive.

| **Lo bueno** es la gente. | The good thing is the people. |
| **Lo malo** es el tránsito. | The bad thing is the traffic. |
| **Lo mejor** fue el asado. | The best part was the asado. |
| **Lo peor** es el calor. | The worst part is the heat. |

**Lo** + adjective makes *the … thing*. It never changes: *lo bueno*, even of a plural.

title_en: Me puse: it happened to you
body_md: **Me puse nervioso**, **me enojé**, **me asusté** — a feeling that came over you at one moment is the preterite. **Estaba nervioso** is the state you were in.
Spanish says you *call yourself*: **me llamo Sofi** — my name is Sofi. Asking someone else: **¿cómo te llamás?**
**Dejame las llaves** — *leave me the keys*; **te dejo** — *I'll leave you (to it)*, the porteño way of hanging up.
**-ito** makes things small, and requests smaller: **un ratito** — *a sec*; **un cafecito**; **un poquito**. It sounds kind rather than childish.
**Lo que pasa es que…** — *the thing is* — explains the real reason. **Lo raro es que…** — *the weird thing is*; **lo importante es que…** — *what matters is*.

title_en: The past, one person at a time
body_md: For anything finished, Buenos Aires uses one past: *laburé* (I worked), *laburaste* (you worked), *laburó* (he/she worked). The stress is what tells *laburo* (I work) from *laburó* (he worked) — the accent is not decoration.
**¿Dónde queda?** — *where is it?* for a place on the map. **Me queda cerca** — *it's close to me*. People **están**; places **quedan**.

title_en: Por un lado, por otro lado
body_md: **Por un lado… por otro lado** weighs two sides. **En cambio** — *whereas* — sets two people or things against each other: *yo laburo, en cambio él no*.

title_en: The irregular ones have no accent
body_md: **Hice, vi, dije, pude, vine** — the pasts you use most carry no accent, unlike *laburé* or *comí*. **¿Qué hiciste?** — **Nada, vi una peli.**
**Estamos atrasados** — *we're behind*. The porteño answer: **no pasa nada, lo sacamos**.
The phone is **el celu** (short for *celular*). **Me quedé sin batería** — *my battery died*; **se cortó** — *it cut out*; **mandame la ubicación** — *send me your location*.

| **Deberías** descansar. | You should rest. |
| **Debería** llamarla. | I should call her. |
| **Estaría bueno** juntarnos. | It'd be nice to get together. |
| **Habría que** avisarle. | We ought to let him know. |

All four take an infinitive. *Tenés que* is an order; *deberías* is advice.
**Creo que viene** — *I think he's coming* — keeps the normal verb. Doubt it and the subjunctive comes in: **no creo que venga**.
**Si hubiera sabido, te hubiera avisado** — both halves take **hubiera**, for something that didn't happen.

| what she said | what you tell |
| «Traeme algo.» | Me pidió que le **trajera** algo. |
| «Esperen.» | Nos dijo que **esperáramos**. |
| «Dejalo acá.» | Me pidió que lo **dejara** acá. |
| «Vení.» | Quería que **viniera**. |

A request or an order told later takes the past subjunctive after **que**. News doesn't: *dijo que venía*.

| what she said | what you tell |
| «¿Venís?» | Me preguntó **si venía**. |
| «Sí.» | Le contesté **que sí**. |

The question comes back with **si**; what was going on slides into the imperfect: *venís* → **venía**.

title_en: Me pidió que, me preguntó si
body_md: A request told later: **me pidió que le trajera algo**. A question: **me preguntó si venía**.
**Te la hago corta** — *long story short* — is usually followed by a long story. **La cuestión es que** — *the thing is* — brings it back on track; **en fin** closes it.

**Como si** — *as if* — always takes the past subjunctive: **habla como si supiera todo**, **como si fuera fácil**. **Como si nada** — *as if nothing had happened*. **¡Ni que fuera tan difícil!** — *it's not like it's that hard!*
**Ir a** + infinitive talks about plans: *Vamos a hacer un asado.* **La semana que viene** is *next week*.
A wish is *que* + the subjunctive: **que te vaya bien** — *good luck, hope it goes well*; **que la pases lindo** — *have a great time*; **que tengas buen finde**.
**Pedir** changes its vowel: **pido** today, **pedí** yesterday, and **pidió** for someone else. **¿Qué pediste?** — **Pedí un bife.**
**Cargar**, **en joda**, **un chiste gracioso** — humour, porteño style.
**A medida que** — *as*, for two things changing together: **a medida que pasa el tiempo, te vas acostumbrando**.

| | comer | vivir |
| yo | com**o** | viv**o** |
| vos | com**és** | viv**ís** |
| él, ella | com**e** | viv**e** |
| nosotros | com**emos** | viv**imos** |
| ellos, ustedes | com**en** | viv**en** |

-er and -ir are the same except for **vos** and **nosotros**, where each keeps its own vowel.
**Fui** is both *I went* (ir) and *I was* (ser). **Fui a la cancha** — *I went to the game*; **fue re lindo** — *it was really nice*. The sentence always tells you which.
Mate goes around the circle and always comes back to whoever is serving it. Saying **gracias** means *I'm done* — only say it when you don't want another round.
**Cargar** someone is *to tease, to wind up*: **¿me estás cargando?** — *are you pulling my leg?* Porteños **cargan** the people they like; being left alone is the bad sign.
For plans porteños say *voy a*. The future tense is for **guessing**: **¿dónde estará?** — *where can he be?*; **estará en el laburo** — *he's probably at work*.
Two pronouns go person first, thing second: **te lo devuelvo** — *I'll give it back to you*. *Le lo* never happens: it turns into **se lo**.
In Argentina the waiter is **el mozo** (or *la moza*). When you're done, ask for **la cuenta**. A **cortado** is an espresso with a dash of milk.
**Según** — *according to*: **según el diario**, **según mi vieja**. **Al parecer** and **supuestamente** keep a distance from what you're passing on.
You don't just ask, you **plantear** it — *raise it, put it on the table*: **le planteé lo del aumento a mi jefa**. Then you **negociar** the **condiciones**.
Regular verbs make the imperfect with **-aba** (*jugaba, laburaba*) or **-ía** (*comía, salía*). Only *nosotros* takes an accent: **jugábamos**, **salíamos**.
**Ir** + *-ando, -iendo* is something happening bit by bit: **voy entendiendo** — *I'm starting to get it*; **se va llenando** — *it's filling up*. **De a poco** — *little by little* — goes with it.
Someone from the city of Buenos Aires is **porteño** or **porteña** — from *puerto*, the port. People from the rest of the country are not.

| yo | estoy | vos | estás |
| él, ella | está | nosotros | **estamos** |
| ellos, ustedes | **están** | | |

The word for the feeling matches the people in number too:

| one man | cansad**o** | one woman | cansad**a** |
| men | cansad**os** | women | cansad**as** |

A word ending in *-e* just adds *-s*: *triste, tristes*. *Feliz* becomes **felices**.
**Me robaron el celu**, **se rompió el calefón** — and who to call for each.
**Acá se saluda con un beso** — *here people greet with a kiss*. **Se** + verb says what everyone does, no subject needed.
More than one: **fueron detenidos** — *they were arrested*. In conversation porteños turn it around: *construyeron el puente*, *los detuvieron*.

| **Me merezco** un aumento. | I deserve a raise. |
| **Me lo merezco.** | I deserve it. |
| **Te lo merecés.** | You deserve it. |

**Merecerse** comes with its pronoun: the bare *merezco* sounds like a textbook.
*Querer* and *poder* change their stem in most forms (*quiero*, *puede*) — but not with vos: **querés**, **podés**. *Ir* is fully irregular: *voy, vas, va, vamos, van*.

A request told later takes the past subjunctive: «Traeme pan» → **me pidió que le trajera pan**; «Esperen» → **nos dijo que esperáramos**. *Dijo que* + subjunctive is an order; *dijo que* + indicative is news.
**Dicen que** — *they say*, *apparently* — is how a porteño passes on anything heard second-hand. **Parece que** does the same with a shrug.
What causes the feeling follows **que** in the subjunctive: **me da bronca que no conteste**, **me da vergüenza que me vean así**.
Working from home is **hacer home office**, in English, and said the Spanish way.
A yes-or-no question told later hangs on **si**: «¿Venís?» → **me preguntó si venía**. *No sé si abre hoy* — *I don't know if it's open today*. **Dudo** — *I doubt it*.
**Deberías** for advice, **estaría bueno** for a gentle suggestion.
At the verdulería the price moves, so it's **¿a cuánto está el kilo?** — *how much is it a kilo today?* You buy **un kilo**, **medio kilo** or **una docena**.
**Había** is *there was, there were*; **hacía calor** is *it was hot*. **Mientras** — *while* — joins two things going on at once.
**Pido** (I order), **pedís** (you order); in the past **pedí**, **pediste**, and — with an *i* — **pidió**. At the table: **¿Me traés la carta?** and, at the end, **la cuenta**.

| a fact — normal verb | a maybe — subjunctive |
| Aunque **llueve**, vamos. | Aunque **llueva**, vamos. |
| Aunque **cuesta**, sigo. | Aunque **cueste**, sigo. |
| Aunque **querés**, no podés. | Aunque no **quieras**, tenés que ir. |

Left: it *is* raining. Right: whether or not it rains. **Igual** at the end — *anyway* — often closes it.

| **Me robaron** el celu. | My phone got stolen. |
| ¿Cuánto te **cobraron**? | How much did they charge you? |
| **Dicen** que mañana llueve. | They say it'll rain tomorrow. |

The *ellos* form with nobody named is how Spanish says *it got done*: no one to blame, or no one worth naming.
Vos keeps the vowel of the infinitive and stresses it: *comer* → **comés**, *vivir* → **vivís**, *leer* → **leés**.
**Antes de que llegue** — *before he gets here* — always takes the subjunctive: it hasn't happened yet.

title_en: No te lo tomes a mal
body_md: Before the hard thing: **no te lo tomes a mal** — *don't take it the wrong way*; **con todo respeto** — *with all due respect*. After it: **no lo dije para ofenderte**.
**Me preguntó si venía** — *she asked me if I was coming*. **Le contesté que sí** — *I told her yes*. What was said slides into the imperfect.
To report it you **hacés la denuncia** at the **comisaría**, or online. The **policía** rarely finds the phone; the denuncia is for the insurance and the new SIM.
**Se casó**, **nació**, **me emocioné** — the news that matters.

Start from the *yo* of the present and swap the vowel: *-ar* verbs take **e**, the rest take **a**.

| yo (now) | vos | yo, él, ella |
| llamo | **llames** | **llame** |
| vengo | **vengas** | **venga** |
| hago | **hagas** | **haga** |
| traigo | **traigas** | **traiga** |
| voy | **vayas** | **vaya** |

*Ir* is the odd one out. It follows **quiero que**: *quiero que vengas*.
Reporting a promise moves it into *would*: «voy» → **dijo que iría**; «te llamo» → **dijo que me llamaría**. Porteños also say **dijo que iba a venir** — same thing.
In Argentina voting is **obligatorio**. **¿A quién votaste?** is a real question, though many answer **eso no se pregunta**. **Votar a** someone: *voté a la misma candidata*.
**Todo aumenta**, **el café subió**, **¿cuánto te cobraron?** — the small talk of prices.
**Había** + a participle is the past behind another past: **cuando llegué, ya habían comido** — *when I got there, they'd already eaten*. Buenos Aires uses this one freely.
A **milonga** is both a dance hall and a faster cousin of the tango. The instrument that sighs is the **bandoneón**.
**Por si** — *just in case* — is the exception: it keeps the normal verb. **Llevá paraguas por si llueve.** Short version: **por las dudas**.
A document that has run out is **vencido**: *tengo el pasaporte vencido*. You **renovás** it, fill in a **formulario**, wait in the **fila**, and **firmás**.
**Me da cosa** — *it makes me uneasy, I don't feel right about it*. **Me pone mal** — *it gets me down*. **Me quedé con las ganas** — *I missed out, and I still want to*.
The easy way to order is to ask the waiter to bring it: **¿Me traés un café?** — literally "do you bring me a coffee?". *Quiero un café* works too. Add **por favor**.
**Funcionar** is *to work* for things: **el subte no funciona**, **los semáforos no funcionan**. For people, it's still *laburar*.
Where English says *used to*, Spanish just uses the imperfect: **Siempre tomaba mate con mi abuela** — *I always used to have mate with my grandma*.
**Estoy laburando** — I'm working (right now). In Argentina, *estoy llegando* can mean you're still ten minutes away.
**Te recomiendo que vayas** — *I'd recommend you go*. **Es mejor que** works the same way: **es mejor que pidas un taxi**.
**Avisame cuando llegás** — *let me know when you get there*. **Te aviso** — *I'll let you know*.
**¿Qué hora será?** — *I wonder what time it is*. **Será** on its own shrugs: *could be*.
**Qué pesado** — *what a pain* — for someone who won't let it go. **Divertido** is *fun*, **tímido** *shy*.
**Es cualquiera** — *that's nonsense*. **Flasheaste** — *you're imagining things*. And a **¡qué lindo!** can be sincere, or ironic when the rain starts.

Spanish tells accidents as if they happened *to* you: **se me cayó** — *I dropped it* (it fell on me); **se me rompió** — *it broke on me*; **se me olvidó** — *I forgot*. Nobody is to blame, which is the point.

| do | don't |
| Vení. | No **vengas**. |
| Andá. | No **vayas**. |
| Decime. | No **me digas**. |
| Tocá. | No **toques**. |
| Olvidate. | No **te olvides**. |

*No* + the subjunctive, and the pronoun moves in front: *preocupate* → **no te preocupes**.
**Y nada** is the porteño *so, yeah*: it fills the pause at the end of a story. **Al toque** — *right away*: **me contestó al toque**.
Something that isn't true now: **si tuviera plata, viajaría** — *if I had money, I'd travel*. The *si* half uses a new form, **tuviera**, **fuera**, **pudiera**.
**Me mudé** — *I moved (house)*; **nos mudamos** — *we moved*. The **mudanza** is the move itself, and always a *quilombo*.
**Nacer** — *to be born*: **¿dónde naciste?**, **el bebé nació ayer**. **Está embarazada** — *she's pregnant*.
**Estoy orgulloso de vos** — *I'm proud of you*. **Agradecido** — *grateful*: **estoy muy agradecida**.
*de + el* always becomes **del**, and *a + el* becomes **al**: *la parada del bondi*, *voy al centro*.

The second verb follows the first into the past:

| now | then |
| Quiero que **vengas**. | Quería que **vinieras**. |
| Te pido que **llames**. | Te pedí que **llamaras**. |
| Me dice que **espere**. | Me dijo que **esperara**. |

The past subjunctive is the *ellos* past with **-ra**: *vinieron* → **viniera**, *hicieron* → **hiciera**. With vos: **vinieras, hicieras, llamaras**.

| Llevo dos años **viviendo** acá. | I've been living here for two years. |
| Hace dos años que **vivo** acá. | (the same) |
| **Sigo** laburando ahí. | I still work there. |
| **Dejé de** fumar. | I quit smoking. |
| **Volvió a** llamar. | He called again. |

English *have been …ing* is the present in Spanish. **Llevar** + time + *-ando, -iendo*.

| | querer | poder | ir |
| yo | quiero | puedo | voy |
| vos | **querés** | **podés** | vas |
| él, ella | quiere | puede | va |
| nosotros | **queremos** | **podemos** | vamos |
| ellos | quieren | pueden | van |

*e → ie* and *o → ue* everywhere except **vos** and **nosotros**. *Ir* is its own thing. Add an infinitive for plans: *¿Querés salir?*

Words that describe someone change for a man or a woman:

| a man | a woman |
| argentin**o** | argentin**a** |
| uruguay**o** | uruguay**a** |
| porteñ**o** | porteñ**a** |
| ingl**és** | ingl**esa** |

*-o* becomes *-a*. A word ending in a consonant adds *-a*, and *inglés* loses its accent: **inglesa**.
Reported promises go into *would*: **dijo que vendría**, **me prometiste que me llamarías**.
**Facturas** are the pastries you buy by the dozen at the bakery — *medialunas* are the best known. Nothing to do with bills.
**Tengo que laburar** is *I have to work*; **hay que** is the same for everyone: **hay que sacar la basura** — *the rubbish has to go out*.
After a match it's **ganamos**, **perdimos** or **empatamos** — *we* won, even if you were on the sofa. The course leaves the club to you.
**Me gustaría** — *I'd like* — is *gustar* in the conditional, with the same *me*: **me gustaría ir**, **¿te gustaría venir?**. **Me encantaría** is the enthusiastic yes.

title_en: The little word goes on the end
body_md: In a request the pronoun sticks to the verb: **llamame**, **mandame**, **dame**, **prestame**. In a statement it goes in front: **te llamo**, **me mandás**.
A negative command is the subjunctive: **no te preocupes**, **no te olvides**, **no digas nada**. **Probá** becomes **no pruebes**.
A **rumor** is just that until someone **confirma**: *el club confirmó la noticia*. Or as porteños say about any rumor: **dicen que…**
With a vos command the pronoun joins the end, and there is no accent: **llamame**, **mandame un audio**, **dame**, **prestame**. *Le* and *les* are *to him, to her, to them*.
A **kiosco** is the corner shop that sells drinks, sweets and bus cards, often through a window onto the street. Many never close.

| **Voy entendiendo.** | I'm starting to get it. |
| **Vas aprendiendo** de a poco. | You're learning bit by bit. |
| **Estoy por** salir. | I'm about to leave. |
| **Está por** llover. | It's about to rain. |

**Ir** + gerund is change in progress; **estar por** + infinitive is what's about to happen.
Add **-s** after a vowel (*medialuna → medialunas*) and **-es** after a consonant. The word for "a" disappears: *una empanada*, but *dos empanadas*.
**No doy más** — *I can't take it anymore*. **No lo aguanto** — *I can't stand him*. And when it's one thing too many: **¡es el colmo!**
One form covers both: **él es** and **ella es**. It also works for a name: *Juan es de Rosario.*

| more than | **más** alto **que** yo |
| less than | **menos** caro **que** |
| as … as | **tan** lindo **como** |
| better, worse | **mejor**, **peor** |
| older, younger | **más grande**, **más chico** |
| very, very | rico → **riquísimo**, caro → **carísimo** |

The describing word still matches the person: *mi hermana es más alta que yo*.
**Según el diario**, **al parecer**, **supuestamente** — passing it on without vouching for it.
**Gracias por todo**, **mil gracias**, **gracias un montón** — the thanks gets bigger, the grammar doesn't change.

| | ser | tener | vivir | ir |
| yo, él, ella | era | tenía | vivía | iba |
| vos | eras | tenías | vivías | ibas |
| nosotros | éramos | | | íbamos |

This past describes: how things *were*, what you *had*, where you *lived*. *Yo* and *él* share one form. **Cuando era chico vivía en Rosario.**

title_en: Lo, la, le — where they go
body_md:
| the thing, masculine | **lo**, **los** | ¿El audio? **Lo** mando ahora. |
| the thing, feminine | **la**, **las** | ¿La tarjeta? **La** tengo. |
| to him, her, them | **le**, **les** | **Le** doy la llave. |
| me, you | **me**, **te** | **Te** llamo mañana. |

Before a normal verb: *la tengo*. Stuck to the end of a command: **llamame**, **dame**, **mandame**.
**Merecerse** — *to deserve* — comes with its pronoun: **me merezco un aumento**, **te lo merecés**. And a boss who **valora** your work says so with the sueldo.
Porteños close the thought with **igual** — *anyway*: *aunque esté cansada, voy igual*. **A pesar de** takes a noun or an infinitive: *a pesar del frío*.
A command with *no* uses the subjunctive: *vení* but **no vengas**, *andá* but **no vayas**, *decime* but **no me digas**. The pronoun moves to the front: **no te preocupes**.
**Reírse** is *to laugh*: **me reí un montón**, **nos reímos de todo**. **Llorar** is *to cry*: **lloré con la película**.

The little word in front changes with the person, and so does the verb:

| yo | **me llamo** | my name is |
| vos | **te llamás** | your name is |

The question puts *cómo* first: **¿Cómo te llamás?** The vos form ends in **-ás**, with the stress on the end.
**Me arrepiento** — *I regret it*; **me arrepentí** — *I regretted it, I changed my mind*. A missed chance is a **oportunidad** you didn't **aprovechar**.
**Casarse** is *to get married*: **se casó**, **nos casamos en marzo**. The wedding is a **casamiento**, and porteño ones end at six in the morning.

title_en: A la that points at nothing
body_md:
| **Se la cree.** | He's full of himself. |
| **Me la banco.** | I can handle it. |
| **Se la bancó.** | She put up with it. |
| **Me las arreglo.** | I get by. |
| **La tenés clara.** | You know your stuff. |

The *la* stays *la* whoever you're talking about; only the verb and the first pronoun change.
Prices **suben** and, now and then, **bajan**. **¿Cuánto te cobraron?** — *how much did they charge you?* A **precio** is a price; *está a buen precio* — *it's a good price*.
**Ni ahí** — *no way, not even close* — is how a porteño turns something down. **Tal cual** — *exactly* — is how they agree.
**Recorrimos la Patagonia**; **¿quién ceba?** — the country and its ritual.

**Che** is how people in Buenos Aires get someone's attention — like "hey". It goes in front, where "hey" goes: *Che, ¿todo bien?* Only a greeting comes before it — *Hola, che.* It is never the English "man" on the end. It's friendly, never rude.
**Ir a** + infinitive talks about plans: *Vamos a hacer un asado.* **La semana que viene** is *next week*.
When your **acento** gives you away less and less, someone will say **ya sos de acá** — *you're one of us now*. Take it: it's the highest praise the city has.

These verbs carry a pronoun that matches the person:

| yo | **me** levanto | **me** acuesto |
| vos | **te** levantás | **te** acostás |
| él, ella | **se** levanta | **se** acuesta |
| nosotros | **nos** levantamos | |

The pronoun goes before the verb. *Acostarse* changes *o → ue*, but not with vos: **te acostás**.
The two biggest teams playing each other is **el superclásico**; any derby is a **clásico**. The fans stand on the **tribuna**. Which side you're on, the course leaves to you.
**Hacer las compras** is doing the food shopping; **sacar la basura** is taking the rubbish out.
**No te hagas problema** — *don't worry about it* — is what a porteño says when you apologise. **No te olvides** — *don't forget*.

The *if* half has its own form. Take the *ellos* past and swap **-ron** for **-ra**:

| tuvie-ron | **tuviera** |
| fue-ron | **fuera** |
| pudie-ron | **pudiera** |
| estuvie-ron | **estuviera** |

Then the other half takes *would*: **si tuviera tiempo, viajaría**. With vos: *si tuvieras*, *¿qué harías?*
**Disculpe**, **pase**, **siéntese**, **quisiera** — the *él* form, for someone you don't tutear… or vosear.
Living in a building means paying **expensas** — *the monthly building fees* — to the **consorcio**. The **encargado** is the building's super, and knows everything.
**Estoy de acuerdo** — *I agree*. Disagreeing: **para nada** — *not at all*; **depende** — *it depends*; **en parte** — *partly*.
**En cambio** sets two things against each other; **de hecho** backs up what you said; **en realidad** corrects it.

| Me da **bronca**. | It makes me mad. |
| Me da **vergüenza**. | I'm embarrassed. |
| Me da **lástima**. | I feel sorry (for him). |
| Me da **igual**. | I don't care. |

The cause follows **que** in the subjunctive: **me da bronca que no avise**. In the past, **me dio**: *me dio vergüenza*.
**Me da miedo** — *it scares me* — works like *gustar*; in a story it's **me dio miedo**. The reaction afterwards: **¡qué susto!**
An asado comes in order: first **chorizo** and **morcilla**, the **achuras**, then the cuts — **vacío**, bife. A **choripán** is a chorizo in bread, the food of every stadium.
**Me toca lavar** — *it's my turn to wash up*. **¿A quién le toca?** Porteños split the chores with *tocar*, never with *turno*.
Meat comes **jugosa** — *pink, juicy* — **a punto** — *medium* — or well done. The **parrilla** is both the grill and the restaurant.
**El que** — *the one that* — matches what it stands for: **el que quieras**, **la que está en la esquina**, **los que vinieron**, **las que prefieras**.
For almost anything official you first **sacás turno** — you book an appointment online — and you bring the **DNI**, the national ID card, without which nothing happens.
**Gardel canta mejor cada día**; the meat comes **jugosa** or **a punto**.

*Ser* — to be — has a form for each person. So far:

| yo | **soy** | I am |
| vos | **sos** | you are |

Use **vos** with everyone: friends, the waiter, your boss. A question is the same words with a rising voice: *¿Sos Sofi?*
*Es la una* (one o'clock), but *son las dos*, *son las siete*. Add **y media** for half past and **y cuarto** for quarter past. *A la noche* means at night.
**Me molesta que llegue tarde** — *it bugs me that he's late*. *Molestar* works like *gustar*.
The city is **la Capital**; the ring of towns around it, in the province, is **el conurbano**. Palermo, San Telmo and La Boca are all barrios of the Capital.
Regular **-ar** verbs: *laburo, laburás, labura, laburamos, laburan*. The vos form stresses the last syllable and carries an accent: *hablás*, *estudiás*.
It works on adverbs too: **cerquita** — *really close*; **despacito** — *nice and slow*. **Chiquito** — *tiny*.
When the wanting is in the past, the second verb moves into the past too: *quiero que vengas* becomes **quería que vinieras** — *I wanted you to come*.
**Conseguí laburo** — *I got a job*. *Conseguir* is the porteño verb for getting anything that took effort: a *turno*, a table, a flat.
**Si hubiera ahorrado, ahora tendría…** — and the regret: **tendría que haber ahorrado**.
*¿Viste?* is also just *you saw*: **¿Viste el partido?** — *Did you see the game?* — the same word porteños drop into every story to mean *you know?*
In the south, **glaciares**; in the north-east, the **cataratas** of Iguazú; in the north-west, Salta's **paisaje** of red hills.
**¿Me pasás la sal?** is how you ask at the table — a question in the present. **¿Podrías…?** is softer, for a bigger favor.

| ¡Qué bueno que **estés** acá! | So good you're here! |
| Qué lástima que no **vengas**. | Shame you're not coming. |
| Me molesta que **llegue** tarde. | It bugs me he's late. |

A reaction to something + **que** → the subjunctive. **Me alegro** on its own: *I'm glad*.

A past that went differently, and what it would mean today: **si hubiera ahorrado** (then), **ahora tendría un depto** (now). The first half is *hubiera* + participle, the second the plain conditional.

| one thing | more than one |
| **Se vende** auto. | **Se venden** bicis. |
| **Se alquila** depto. | |
| **Se necesita** mozo. | |

**Se** + the *él* form, or the *ellos* form for plurals. Nobody is named: it's what's being sold, rented, needed.
**Lo** + adjective is *the … thing*: **lo bueno** — *the good thing*; **lo malo** — *the bad thing*; **lo mejor** and **lo peor**. **Lo bueno de vivir acá es que…**
**Cuanto más** — *the more*: **cuanto más practicás, mejor hablás**. **Cuanto menos** — *the less*. And **cuanto antes** — *the sooner the better*: **avisame cuanto antes**.
**Navidad** falls in the heat, so it is often an *asado*, cider and **pan dulce** at midnight, and a **brindis** — *¡salud!* — before the fireworks.
*Ir* and *ser* share their past: **fui, fuiste, fue**. *Fui a la cancha* — *I went to the stadium*; *fue bárbaro* — *it was great*. The rest of the sentence tells which.
**Hay** introduces something: *Hay un kiosco* — there's a kiosco. **Está** says where something you already know about is: *El kiosco está en la esquina.*
**Deberías** — *you should* — is advice with the edges sanded off: **deberías descansar**. **Debería** is *I should* or *he should*: *debería llamar a mi vieja*.
Porteños talk about the future with **ir a**: **voy a laburar**, **vamos a comer**. *Next week* is **la semana que viene**, *next year* **el año que viene**.

| the scene — imperfect | what happened — preterite |
| **Estaba** en el subte | cuando me **llamó** Sofi. |
| **Llovía** mucho | y **llegué** tarde. |
| **Había** mucha gente | y no **pude** entrar. |

Ask: was it going on, or did it happen? Going on → *-aba, -ía*. Happened, and finished → the preterite.
Most porteños have an **abuelo** or **bisabuelo** who **llegó en barco** from Italy or Spain. That's why a porteño talks with his hands and eats ñoquis on the 29th.
**Más caro que**, **menos lejos que** — *more expensive than*, *less far than*. **Tan lindo como** is *as nice as*. *Better* and *worse* have their own words: **mejor**, **peor**.
**Hay** introduces something: *Hay un kiosco* — there's a kiosk. **Está** says where something you already know about is: *El kiosco está en la esquina.*
**Como si** takes the past subjunctive: *como si supiera*. **El que, la que** — *the one that*: *la que prefieras*.
**Estoy harto** — *I'm fed up*; porteños go further: **estoy podrido** — literally *rotten*. Both take **de**: **harta del tránsito**, **podrido del ruido**.

title_en: Hay que, tenés que, no hace falta
body_md: **Hay que** is *it has to be done* — nobody in particular. **Tenés que** is *you have to*. **No hace falta** is *there's no need*.
Use **estar** for where someone or something is: *¿Dónde estás?* *El kiosco está acá.* It is a different verb from *ser*, which says what something is.
**Llevo dos años viviendo acá** — *I've been living here for two years*. Where English says *have been …ing*, Spanish stays in the present: **hace dos años que vivo acá** says the same.

| Voy, **a menos que llueva**. | unless |
| Voy, **siempre y cuando vengas**. | as long as |
| Llamame **en caso de que haya** un problema. | in case |
| Llevá paraguas **por si llueve**. | just in case |

The first three take the subjunctive. **Por si** is the exception: normal verb.
Porteño advice starts with **yo que vos** — *if I were you* — and goes straight to the conditional: **yo que vos, no le diría nada**.

**Tener que** + an infinitive — the *-ar, -er, -ir* form — is *to have to*:

| Tengo que laburar. | I have to work. |
| ¿Tenés que estudiar? | Do you have to study? |

Jobs change for a woman: *profesor* → **profesora**, *médico* → **médica**, *jefe* → **jefa**. And no *un, una*: **Soy abogada.**
**Resulta que** — *it turns out* — is how a porteño story takes its turn. **Encima** — *on top of that* — makes it worse: **encima, llovía**. **Total** shrugs it off: **total, nadie se dio cuenta**.

title_en: Ser and tener, all of them
body_md:
With *nosotros* and *ellos*, both verbs are complete:

| | ser | tener |
| yo | soy | tengo |
| vos | sos | tenés |
| él, ella | es | tiene |
| nosotros | **somos** | **tenemos** |
| ellos, ustedes | **son** | **tienen** |

**Ustedes** — *you all* — uses the *ellos* form. Argentina never uses *vosotros*.
The subjunctive after **que** for what you haven't found (*un depto que tenga balcón*) and for what makes you feel something (*me da bronca que no avise*).
**De hecho** — *in fact* — backs up what you just said. **En realidad** — *actually* — corrects it: *en realidad no es tan caro*. **Por eso** — *that's why*.
Renting in Buenos Aires means the **inmobiliaria** asks for a **garantía** — a relative's property as a guarantee — and a **contrato**. Some **dueños** don't take **mascotas**.
**Chabón**, **mina**, **groso**, **birra**, **trucho** — among friends.
A porteño argues hard and softens it: **puede ser, pero…** — *could be, but…*
**No es que no quiera** (subjunctive), **es que no puedo** (normal verb).
**Paro**, **corte**, **piquete** — and the street **está cortada**.
**¡Ojo!** — literally *eye!* — is *careful!, watch out!*: **ojo, que no es tan fácil**. **Estoy seguro** — *I'm sure*; **no estoy segura** — *I'm not sure*.
**No me alcanza** — *it's not enough*, *I can't make it last*. **Ahorrar** is to save, **gastar** to spend: **gasté todo el sueldo**.
A fan is a **hincha**, and a **gol** is shouted, not said.

Most family words come in pairs:

| man | woman |
| herman**o** | herman**a** |
| hij**o** | hij**a** |
| abuel**o** | abuel**a** |
| novi**o** | novi**a** |
| viej**o** | viej**a** |

**Mi** — *my* — never changes: *mi hermano*, *mi hermana*. And *papá* ends in *-a* but is a man.
**Lograr** — *to manage, to pull off*: **¡lo lograste!** — *you did it!* **Felicitaciones** is how the course says it; **¡grande!** is how a porteño would.

The first question in a new friendship. A team is a **cuadro**, and you don't choose it, you inherit it: **soy del mismo cuadro que mi viejo**. To root for one is **hinchar por**: **¿por quién hinchás?**
The verbs you use most have their own past: **hice** (I did), **vi** (I saw), **dije** (I said), **vine** (I came), **pude** (I could). No accent on any of them.
Change the middle word for the person: **se te cayó** — *you dropped it*; **se le rompió** — *he broke it*.
**Ya no** — not anymore; **cada vez más** — more and more. And when it's too much: **estoy podrido**.
Porteños go on **vacaciones** in January and February, and *la costa* — Mar del Plata, Pinamar — is where half of Buenos Aires ends up.
A porteño **maneja** (drives) an **auto** and spends half an hour trying to **estacionar** (park). *Conducir* and *aparcar* are Spain's.
**Medio** in front of an adjective softens it — *estoy medio cansado*, I'm kind of tired. It never changes: *medio cansada* too.
Most end in **-ado** or **-ido**: *comido, llegado, salido*. A few don't: **hecho**, **dicho**, **visto**, **roto**.
**Me hizo reír**, **me hace acordar**, and **cuanto más practicás, mejor**.
The ATM is **el cajero** — you go **a sacar plata**. Most porteños split the bill by **transferencia**: **te transfiero** — *I'll transfer it to you*.
**Me quejé** — *I complained*; **¿de qué te quejás?** — *what are you complaining about?* **Reclamar** is to file a complaint, and something you do a lot with a phone company.

| Que te vaya bien. | Good luck. |
| Que la pases lindo. | Have a great time. |
| Que tengas buen finde. | Have a good weekend. |
| Ojalá que no llueva. | I hope it doesn't rain. |
| Ojalá salga todo bien. | I hope it all works out. |

A wish is **que** or **ojalá** + the subjunctive. *Tener → tengas, salir → salga*: the *g* of *tengo, salgo* comes along.
**Vino** is wine, and it is also *he came*: **vino Juan** — *Juan came*. The sentence always tells which.

title_en: The words that glue a conversation
body_md: **Por las dudas** — *just in case*; **de última** — *if all else fails*; **en serio** — *seriously*; **si querés** — *if you like*. Say them and you sound like you're from here.

title_en: Then, and what it means now
body_md:
| if (then) | now |
| Si **hubiera ahorrado**, | ahora **tendría** un depto. |
| Si **hubiéramos** salido antes, | ya **estaríamos** ahí. |
| Si **hubiera aceptado**, | ahora **sería** otra cosa. |

*Hubiera* + participle for the past that didn't happen; the plain conditional for today.
When the story ends badly, the answer is **¡Qué garrón!** — *what a drag!* Informal, and everywhere.
**A menos que** takes the subjunctive (*a menos que llueva*); **por si** doesn't (*por si llueve*).
A **chabón** is a guy, a **mina** a woman — among friends; both sound rude to strangers. Someone great at what they do is a **groso**; a **birra** is a beer.

| same person — infinitive | someone else — subjunctive |
| Estudio **para aprender**. | Te lo explico **para que entiendas**. |
| | Te lo mando **para que lo leas**. |
| | Avisame **antes de que** llegue. |

**Antes de que** always takes the subjunctive: it hasn't happened yet.
**Contame** opens it; **de repente** is the twist, **por suerte** the relief, **al final** the end. **Igual** — *anyway* — goes almost anywhere, and **o sea** is *I mean*.

The preterite says what happened; the **imperfect** says what things were like: **era** (I was / he was), **tenía** (I had), **vivía** (I lived), **iba** (I went, I used to go). *Cuando era chico vivía en Rosario* — both verbs describe, nothing *happens*.
**-ito** softens: **un ratito**, **un cafecito**, **cerquita**.
A machine that doesn't work **no anda**: **no anda el ascensor**, **el wifi no anda**. **Funciona** is correct, but it's what the manual says.
**Me cayó la ficha** — *the penny dropped* — comes from the old phone tokens that fell when the call went through. **Recién ahora me cayó la ficha** — *it only just sank in*.

| a masculine thing | **el que** quieras |
| a feminine thing | **la que** está en la esquina |
| more than one | **los que** vinieron, **las que** prefieras |
| a place | el bar **donde** nos conocimos |

It matches what it stands for. *El que quieras* — whichever you want — takes the subjunctive: you haven't chosen yet.
**Sé** — *I know* — has an accent to tell it from *se*. **¿Sabés qué?** — *you know what?* — opens every piece of gossip.
A porteño asks with a plain question in the present: **¿me pasás la sal?**, **¿me ayudás?** — the *can you* is in the tone. **¿Podrías…?** is the extra-polite version.
A porteño goodbye is several: **bueno, nos hablamos**, **cuidate**, **un beso**, **que descanses** — and then another *chau* at the door.
**Me quedé sin batería**, **sin plata**, **sin laburo** — *I ran out of*. It is the preterite: it happened at one moment.
**Me puse nervioso** — *I got nervous*; **se puso contenta** — *she got happy*. The feeling changes, so it's *ponerse*, in the preterite.
**Lo de** is *the business with*: **¿qué pasó con lo de Juan?** And **lo de siempre** is *the usual*: at the café, at the bar, in life.
**Lo que** is *what* in the middle of a sentence: **¿viste lo que pasó?**, **no sé lo que quiere**.

| **Me hizo reír.** | It made me laugh. |
| **Me hizo llorar.** | It made me cry. |
| **Me hace acordar** a vos. | It reminds me of you. |

**Hacer** + infinitive is *to make someone do it*. The person goes in front: **me**, **te**, **nos**.
Agreeing with something positive: **A mí también.** Agreeing with something negative: **A mí tampoco.**
**Devolveme las llaves**, **dejame pasar**, **traeme el cargador** — in requests the pronoun rides on the end, and it's always *me*.
**Extraño a mi vieja** — *I miss my mum*. Not *echar de menos*: that is Spain's, and here nobody says it.
**Emocionarse** is *to be moved, to get emotional* — never just *excited*: **me emocioné en el casamiento**. **Se me puso la piel de gallina** — *I got goosebumps*.
**Llevo un rato esperando** — *I've been waiting a while*. **Sigo esperando** — *I'm still waiting*.
**¿Te acordás cuando…?** opens every memory at a family asado. **Me acuerdo** — *I remember*; **no me acuerdo** — *I don't remember*.

title_en: How a vos command is made
body_md:
Take the infinitive, drop the *-r*, and stress the last vowel:

| mirar | **mirá** |
| esperar | **esperá** |
| venir | **vení** |
| andar | **andá** |

A pronoun joins the end, and the accent goes, because the stress doesn't move: *esperá* → **esperame**. *Decir* → **decime**, *sentarse* → **sentate**.
**Hacerse el** + a describing word is *to act, to play*: **se hace el vivo** — *he acts all clever*; **se hizo el distraído** — *he pretended not to notice*.
**Lo que pasa es que**, **lo raro es que**, **lo de siempre** — and a **dicho** to close it.
**Era**, **tenía**, **estaba** paint the scene — how things were. **Fui**, **tuve**, **llegó** are what happened in it. **Estaba lloviendo cuando llegó Juan.**
Spain says *hoy he trabajado*; a porteño says **hoy laburé**. Even for today, even for something that just happened: **¿Llegaste?** — *Did you get here?*
**Resulta que** turns the story, **encima** makes it worse, **total** shrugs.
**No entiendo** — *I don't understand*. **¿Me explicás?** or **explicame** — *can you explain?*
**La previa** is the drinks before going out; **la sobremesa** is the long chat at the table after eating, which nobody cuts short.
You ask for a **turno** (an appointment); the **guardia** is the emergency room. **Estoy engripado** — *I've got the flu* — is what gets you the day off.
Pass on news without owning it: **dicen que va a llover** — *they say it's going to rain*; **parece que Juan se mudó** — *looks like Juan moved*.
**Hace calor**, **hace frío** — it's hot, it's cold. Seasons are flipped: *el verano* runs from December to February.
**Tener que** + infinitive says what you have to do: *Tengo que laburar*, *¿tenés que estudiar?*
**Soler** is *to usually*: **suelo almorzar tarde** — *I usually have lunch late*; **¿solés venir acá?** It only ever comes with an infinitive.
**Estoy laburando** — I'm working (right now). In Argentina, *estoy llegando* can mean you're still ten minutes away.
In Argentina the everyday word for "you" is **vos**, and it has its own verb forms: *vos sos* (you are). You'll hear *tú* in other countries. This course never uses it.
The **calefón** heats the water, and breaks in July. When there's a **pérdida** — *a leak* — you call the **plomero** to **arreglar** it.
The news likes the passive: **fue** + participle. **El puente fue construido en 1900**; **la estación fue inaugurada ayer**. The participle agrees like an adjective: *construido, construida*.
To say where someone is from, put **de** after the verb: *Soy de Rosario.* *¿De dónde sos?*

title_en: Yo and él share a form
body_md: In the imperfect, *yo* and *él/ella* are the same word: **era** is *I was* and *he was*. The subject — or the story — tells you which. **De chico** is *as a kid*.

| Habla **como si supiera** todo. | He talks as if he knew everything. |
| **Como si fuera** fácil. | As if it were easy. |
| Me saludó **como si nada**. | He said hi as if nothing had happened. |
| ¡**Ni que fuera** tan difícil! | It's not like it's that hard! |

After **como si** and **ni que**, always the *-ra* form, whatever the time.
**Voy entendiendo** — bit by bit. **Me cae bien** — I like him, as a person.
Drop the final *-r* and stress the last vowel: *mirar* → **mirá**, *venir* → **vení**. Pronouns stick to the end: **sentate**, **decime**, **esperame**.
**Ojalá** is *I hope*, and the subjunctive follows it: **ojalá que no llueva** — *I hope it doesn't rain*.
In Buenos Aires prices **aumentan** so often that the word is small talk: **¿viste cómo aumentó el café?** The **aumento** of your salary never quite keeps up with the **inflación**.
**Sigo laburando ahí** — *I still work there*. **Dejé de fumar** — *I quit smoking*. **Volvió a llamar** — *he called again*.
**Estoy saliendo con alguien** — *I'm seeing someone*. When it ends, porteños **cortan**: **cortamos** — *we broke up*.
Porteños say **vos** to almost everyone, but **usted** to an older stranger, a doctor, a building's owner. Usted takes the *él* form of the verb: **¿usted es el dueño?**, **pase**, **siéntese**.

| El puente **fue construido** hace un siglo. | was built |
| La estación **fue inaugurada** ayer. | was opened |
| Los chorros **fueron detenidos**. | were arrested |

**Fue** + participle, and the participle agrees like an adjective. In conversation: *construyeron el puente*.
**Me gusta el mate** means "mate pleases me". The verb matches the thing you like: *me gusta el café*, but *me gustan las facturas*.
**Leí en el diario que…**, **lo vi en la tele** — and **me llamó Sofi y me dijo que…**
A work email opens with **Estimado Juan** or **Estimada Sofi** and ends with **Saludos**. **Te adjunto** is *I'm attaching*; **desde ya, gracias** is *thanks in advance*.
The thing that hurts is the subject: **me duele la cabeza** — *my head hurts*, **me duelen los pies** — *my feet hurt*. The *me* says whose, so Spanish uses *la*, not *mi*.
The conditional adds **-ía** to the whole infinitive: *comprar* → **compraría**. A few shorten first: **haría**, **diría**, **tendría**, **podría**.
**Te banco** — *I've got your back*; **no lo banco** — *I can't stand him*. One verb, and porteños use it for both.
**Mis abuelos llegaron de Italia en barco** — otra **época**.

| Te devuelvo **el libro**. | Te **lo** devuelvo. |
| ¿Me dejás **las llaves**? | ¿Me **las** dejás? |
| Le regalé **un libro**. | **Se lo** regalé. |

The person goes first, the thing second. *Le* or *les* before *lo, la* becomes **se**.
A porteño's older sister is *mi hermana **más grande***, the younger one *mi hermano **más chico***. And *-ísimo* turns anything up: **riquísimo**, **carísimo**.

| «¿Venís?» | Me preguntó **si** venía. |
| «¿Abre hoy?» | No sé **si** abre hoy. |
| | **A ver si** nos juntamos. |

A yes-or-no question told later hangs on **si**, with the normal verb.

| vos | usted |
| ¿Vos sos el dueño? | ¿**Usted** es el dueño? |
| Pasá. | **Pase**. |
| Sentate. | **Siéntese**. |
| Disculpá. | **Disculpe**. |

Usted takes the *él* form. **Quisiera** — *I'd like* — works with both.
A reason you deny takes the subjunctive: **no es que no quiera** — *it's not that I don't want to*. The real reason follows with **es que** and the normal verb: **es que no puedo**.
**Tipo** before a time is *around*: **tipo ocho** — *around eight*, which in Buenos Aires means eight-fifteen at the earliest. **En punto** is *on the dot*, and rarer.

| ser | **será** | ¿Qué hora será? |
| estar | **estará** | Estará en el laburo. |
| tener | **tendrá** | Tendrá treinta años. |
| haber | **habrá** | Habrá mucha gente. |

For plans, porteños say *voy a*. This future is for wondering and guessing: *I wonder…*, *he's probably…*
**El que avisa no traiciona** — *I warned you*, literally *who warns doesn't betray*.
The *colectivo* crosses the city; to go to another city you take the **micro** (the coach). You buy the **pasaje** at the terminal or online.
The word for "the" matches its noun: **el** kiosco, **la** esquina, **los** kioscos, **las** esquinas.
**Alguien** is *someone*, **nadie** is *nobody* — and Spanish keeps the *no* as well: **no vino nadie**.
**Lo dije en joda** — *I was joking*. A **chiste** is a joke you tell; if it lands, it's **gracioso**.
**Ya había comido** — *I had already eaten* — puts one past before another: **cuando llegaste, ya había comido**.
**¡Qué bueno que estés acá!** — reacting to something *now* takes the subjunctive. **Me alegro** — *I'm glad*; **qué lástima** — *what a shame*.
**Te debo una** — *I owe you one*. The answer is **de nada**, or, more porteño, **no pasa nada**.
Porteños say a feeling *gives* them something: **me da bronca** — *it makes me mad*; **me da vergüenza** — *I'm embarrassed*; **me da lástima** — *I feel sorry*; **me da igual** — *I don't care*.
**Me pidió que lo llamara** — *she asked me to call him*. The same form follows an order told later: **me dijo que esperara** — *he told me to wait*.
**al lado de** (next to), **enfrente de** (across from), **entre** (between). Remember *de + el* = *del*: *al lado del kiosco*.
**Las elecciones** — *the elections* — decide the **gobierno** and the **presidente**. The course stays out of it: the words, not the opinions.
**¡Mirá vos!** — *well, would you look at that* — and **no lo puedo creer** keep the story going. A **chusma** is someone who loves the gossip.
**Buena onda** is the porteño compliment for a person: easy, warm, *nice*. **Mala onda** is the opposite. Both stay the same for everyone: *ella es buena onda*.

| **No es que** no **quiera**, | It's not that I don't want to, |
| **es que** no puedo. | it's just that I can't. |
| **No es que** no **tengamos** ganas. | It's not that we don't feel like it. |

The reason you deny takes the subjunctive; the real one, after **es que**, the normal verb.
**A ver si** is *let's see if* — and, just as often, a hope: **a ver si nos juntamos** — *we should get together sometime*. To find something out, porteños **averiguan**.

| something new | something you already know |
| **Hay** un kiosco. | **El** kiosco **está** en la esquina. |
| **Hay** una parada acá. | **La** parada **está** lejos. |

**Hay** goes with *un, una* or a number, and never changes: *hay dos subtes*. **Está** goes with *el, la*.
**Tipo** makes a time loose: **tipo ocho** is *around eight*, and in Buenos Aires that means eight-thirty. For exactly eight, say **a las ocho en punto**.
At work, a **proyecto** has a **plazo** — *a deadline* — and a **presupuesto** — *a budget*. You **entregás** it to the **cliente**, ideally before you're **atrasado**.
About something that hasn't happened yet, *cuando* takes the subjunctive: **avisame cuando llegues** — *let me know when you get there*. About a habit it doesn't: *cuando llego, tomo mate*.
**Antes era distinto** — *it used to be different*. **¡Qué épocas!** — *those were the days!* — closes it.
**Laburar** is the everyday Argentine word for *to work* — from the Italian *lavorare*. *Trabajar* is understood everywhere and fine too.

title_en: A menos que, siempre y cuando
body_md: Conditions that haven't happened take the subjunctive: **a menos que llueva** — *unless it rains*; **siempre y cuando vengas** — *as long as you come*; **en caso de que** — *in case*.
**Mejor** and **peor** never take *más*: **está mejor**, **fue peor**. And *-ísimo* is the porteño way to say *really*: **riquísimo**, **carísimo**.
The porteño *how did it go?* is **¿Cómo te fue?**, and the answer is **Me fue bien** or **Me fue re mal**.

With a verb, *gusta* stays singular, even for two activities:

| Me gusta bailar. | Me gusta leer y cocinar. |
| Me encanta el fútbol. | Me encantan las series. |

Agreeing: **A mí también** after a *yes*, **A mí tampoco** after a *no*.

*Comer* and *salir* take the same endings: **comí, comiste, comió**; **salí, saliste, salió**. For *nosotros* the past looks like the present — *salimos* — and *anoche* or *ayer* says which one it is.
Saying **gracias** when you hand the mate back means *I'm done*. Say it on the first one and that's your last.
**Me cayó la ficha**, **me da cosa**, **me pone mal** — feelings in porteño.
A **dicho** is a saying, and porteños drop one to close an argument: **más vale tarde que nunca**; **no hay mal que por bien no venga** — *every cloud has a silver lining*.

| | -ar | -er, -ir |
| yo, él, ella | jug**aba** | com**ía** |
| vos | jug**abas** | com**ías** |
| nosotros | jug**ábamos** | sal**íamos** |

Every verb but *ser, ir* and *ver* follows this. It's the *used to* of English: **Los sábados jugábamos a la pelota.**
**Si tuviera plata, viajaría.** The *if* half takes *tuviera, fuera, pudiera*; the other half takes *-ía*: *iría, haría, sería*.

| one person (vos) | more than one (ustedes) |
| pasá | **pasen** |
| esperá | **esperen** |
| vení | **vengan** |
| traé | **traigan** |
| sentate | **siéntense** |
| no te preocupes | **no se preocupen** |

-ar verbs end in **-en**, the rest in **-an**. The pronoun is **se**, stuck on the end — and then the accent appears: **siéntense, quédense**.
These words change with the person: **argentino** for a man, **argentina** for a woman. Same for *uruguayo / uruguaya*, *chileno / chilena*.
**Mi viejo** and **mi vieja** — literally "my old one" — are affectionate Argentine words for *my dad* and *my mum*.
For where a place *is*, porteños say **queda**: **¿dónde queda la farmacia?** — *where's the chemist?* — and **me queda cerca** — *it's close to me*.
Your health insurance is your **obra social**; the doctor writes a **receta** and you take the **pastillas** **cada ocho horas**.
**Me cae bien** is *I like him* — as a person, not romantically. It works like *gustar*: **me cae bien Juan**, **me caen bien tus amigos**. The first impression: **me cayó mal**.
**Tendría que haber** + participle is *I should have*: **tendría que haber ido**, **tendrías que haber avisado**. Porteños use it far more than any other past regret.

title_en: Se la cree, me la banco
body_md: **Se la cree**, **me la banco**, **me las arreglo**, **la tenés clara** — a *la* that points at nothing.
A word ending in **-o** is usually masculine and takes *un*: *un hermano*. One ending in **-a** is usually feminine and takes *una*: *una hermana*.
Argentines say **depto** for an apartment, **pieza** for a bedroom and **el living** for the living room. The fridge is **la heladera**.
**No hay nada como** — *there's nothing like*: **no hay nada como un asado con amigos**.
Signs say what's done without saying who: **se vende** — *for sale*; **se alquila** — *for rent*; **se necesita mozo** — *waiter wanted*. More than one thing: **se venden bicis**.
With *we*: **si hubiéramos salido antes, ya estaríamos ahí**. The participles: **ahorrado, comprado, vendido, aceptado**.
**¿Cuánto sale?** is the everyday Argentine way to ask a price — *¿cuánto cuesta?* works too. **Mangos** is slang for pesos.
**Depende**, **puede ser**, **en parte** — the porteño hedge. Full agreement is **estoy de acuerdo**; full disagreement, **para nada**.
**Hubiera** takes the participles *había* does: **sabido, venido, ido, llamado, dicho, hecho**. **Si hubieras venido** — *if you had come*.
